i. Abstract
The ME06 Electric Powered Boat project focuses on designing, building and racing an
unmanned boat designed to operate below a maximum system voltage of 55.5V and a battery
capacity of 500 Ah. The vessel must carry a 60 lb. removeable payload around a 2-mile course with
one 180-degree turn. Our team’s performance targets include a foundational goal of 15-20 mph
average speed for the duration of the race and a stretch goal of 45-50 mph, enabling a projected 3minute completion time.
This report presents mechanical and simulated progress across propulsion, water stability,
hydrodynamics, and system integration. Baseline CFD analysis for a 6-blade propeller at 500 RPM
produced thrust and torque values of 4.53x10 3 N and 7.73x104 Nm respectively. These results form
the benchmark against which our 2 and 3 blade propellers will be evaluated to optimize thrust,
torque demand, and wake uniformity. Stability analysis using SolidWorks established the boat’s
center of gravity at (-0.081534, 75.694286, 115.136168) cm, and a center of buoyancy at (0.0000,
72.17918, 125.293628) cm.
Risk assessments identified key threats, including winter weather during testing, battery
failure/explosion, and delays in part shipments. A detailed project schedule outlines thermal
system CAD completion before intersession, full mechanical/electrical integration in early spring,
and iterative Bay Tests to validate all systems before transportation and racing on judgement day.

UCONN

Background
The outdrive assembly was fitted to the stern of the boat before last year’s competition. The
outdrive was removed, inspected for damage, cleaned, and reattached in the same manner. There
were no problems with the outdrive itself during last year’s competition, so all components
considering the outdrive will be kept the same. The single motor system was upgraded to a dual
motor setup with the addition of a gearbox at the top of the outdrive. The electrical team
manufactured the battery with the intent to power two identical motors of shape, size, rotational
output, and brand. The mechanical team fit all other electrical components, including the steering
servo and electric water-cooling pump to the existing hull with loose connections and was
prepared to be integrated into the battery-receiver system created by the electrical team. Once all
electrically powered components were retrofitted to the hull, the electrical team installed the
battery and connected all necessary components as the team saw fit. The boat was also sanded
and repainted as it was last year. The paint and finish used in last year’s competition was not
sufficient in lasting through testing or storage, so research was done to find adequate paints and
finishes for a marine application, such as this year’s boat.

Requirements
i.

Objectives
The primary objective on race day is to complete the course in the shortest possible time.

The strategy is to get the boat to plane and maintain its position for the entirety of the race. When a
J-Class Hydroplane (the type of hull being used) is on plane, the drag on the bottom of the hull is
greatly reduced. With this reduced drag, higher motor RPMs and thus a higher top speed can be
achieved.

ii.

Metrics
The goal was to reach a top speed of 50 mph on the straight aways with an average speed of

40 mph including building speed in the beginning and reducing/regaining speed around the turn
which occurs roughly halfway through the race. Assuming the boat reaches an average speed of 40
MPH, the 2-mile course should be completed in about 3 minutes. Also, the battery may not exceed
60°C to keep the battery functional for extended periods of time. 1

iii.

Constraints
Just as with most engineering design efforts, there are many constraints that must be

navigated during the design and testing process. The four main factors that affect the team
negatively are time, money, weather, and transportation. Time is one of the most critical
constraints. It is challenging to fit the entire process of designing the boat, ordering and receiving
parts, installing components, and testing the completed system within a single school year. This
process must happen multiple times this year when modifying the vessel after testing. Funding also
presents a significant constraint. Although the sponsors are very helpful in funding the project,
many of the high-output electrical components that cannot be made from scratch in one year’s
time are very expensive. In collaboration with the ECE team, efforts are focused on minimizing
costs and manufacturing components, such as the battery, in-house. On the Mechanical side,
there are many small to medium costs such as waterproofing, paint, cooling systems, gearing
systems etc. that all add up very quickly when not planned for in the design stages of the project.
Specific to this project are the constraints imposed by weather conditions and transportation
logistics. To get real world testing data, the boat must be transported to Coventry Lake, which is
about 15 minutes from the storage facility at the depot campus, using the UConn School of
Engineering box truck that is not always available. Weather conditions during the winter months
pose additional challenges, as temperatures in the areas surrounding UConn often remain below
freezing for extended periods. Outdoor testing of the boat during most of the winter and early spring
will not be possible. In anticipation of these limitations, plans have been made to test certain
systems of the boat indoors in pools or other more specialized testing facilities to gain knowledge
about more individualized parts of the system. This specialized testing will not only make effective
use of the limited warm period available in the spring semester before race day but will also
enhance the ability to diagnose and resolve system issues more efficiently.

iv.

Criteria

A superior boat design would be determined by evaluating how effectively it meets
performance, efficiency, reliability, and competition objectives. Key criteria include propulsion
capability, such as using dual motors to increase available power, improving acceleration, and
providing redundancy in case of component failure. Propeller geometry and shaft angle are also
important, as optimizing prop angle and diameter can improve thrust efficiency while minimizing
drag. Battery configuration is another critical factor; arranging the battery to maximize discharge

Additional considerations include overall hull efficiency, system reliability, ease of
maintenance, thermal management of electrical components, and compliance with competition
rules. Ultimately, the better design is the one that delivers higher performance and efficiency with
minimal energy loss while maintaining safety, reliability, and controllability throughout the race.

Hydrodynamics and Drag Reduction
To reach the target speed goals for the design, the total resistance acting on the
hydroplane’s hull must be minimized. When a boat moves through water, the total drag opposing
motion can be divided into two main components: frictional resistance and wave-making
resistance. Frictional resistance results from viscous shear forces as water flows along the hull
surface, while wave-making resistance is caused by the energy required to displace water and
generate surface waves. Molland et al. describe this distinction, noting that “resistance is
categorized into two primary types: frictional resistance, caused by the interaction of water with
the ship’s surface, and wave-making resistance, which arises from the energy required to form and
maintain the hull’s wave system” [1]. Both forms of resistance are significant; as speed increases,
they collectively demand more propulsive power, limiting overall efficiency and stability.
Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) simulations allow these two resistance components
to be visualized and quantified, helping identify which geometric features of the hull contribute
most to total drag. By evaluating how pressure and viscous forces distribute across the wetted
surface, areas that produce high resistance can be refined through design iterations. This analysis
also provides guidance on how to modify hull geometry—such as incorporating trim tabs or
adjusting deadrise angles—to balance lift and drag at planing speeds.
Hoerner [2] states that “the drag of any body in a moving fluid is proportional to the dynamic
pressure, one-half of the product of fluid density and the square of the velocity, multiplied by a
characteristic area and a dimensionless coefficient depending on shape and flow conditions.” This
relationship forms the foundation for all drag prediction methods, including those applied in
marine hydrodynamics. The equation can be seen in Appendix A, equation (1).
For marine applications, this relationship is typically expressed using a total resistance
coefficient, 𝐶𝑇 , which represents the combined effects of both viscous and wave-making

UCONN
components. Molland et al. [1] explain that the resistance experienced by a ship is conventionally
expressed in terms of a non-dimensional coefficient, 𝐶𝑇 , which is represented by equation (2)
appendix A. This marine-specific formulation maintains the same physical meaning as the general
drag equation but relates directly to the wetted hull area, a critical parameter in hull design.
Both expressions convey that the resistance scales with the square of velocity and is
severely impacted by the hull shape and surface area. Even small reductions in 𝐶𝑇 can lead to
notable performance gains as the speed is increased. Adjusting hull geometry and maintaining
laminar flow are key strategies in reducing drag. CFD analysis will be guided through these ideas to
decrease the drag coefficient through smoother flow transitions and reduced wave generation from
the water hitting the hull surface.

Propeller and Propulsion Optimization
Deciding which propeller to use is critical in getting the best performance out of the design.
CFD analysis is the best way to determine this as well as actual physical testing. Yilmaz et al. wrote
that numerical simulations could predict thrust and torque within a 5-10% degree of the
experimental results, which validates the capability of CFD methods to accurately model the
propeller performance [3]. This small error percentage conveys the reliability of the CFD models in
relation to tested results. Previous conclusions about propeller performance through CFD models
can be taken as accurate data. Even though there is variability among different variations of
propellers and CFD software, it is still a useful tool to gain a benchmark for expected performance.
Breslin et al. describes how propeller efficiency represents the ratio of useful work done to total
energy supplied... it is governed by the balance between induced velocity in the slipstream and
viscous losses on the blades [4]. The ratio that was explained is shown in Equation 3, Appendix A.

An extremely important system that the boat needs to function correctly is the steering
system. Although the course only has one turn, at the halfway point, maintaining control over the
vessels heading at all times is essential. Even if the boat were to begin its course perfectly aligned,
external factors such as wind and current can cause the boat to veer off course easily. Last year's
design included a cheap and minimally effective system made up of one electric linear actuator
that turned the entire outdrive system. This actuator was not very powerful and would turn the
outdrive extremely slowly. To remedy this issue, a more advanced steering system was

pages.text:
UCONN
implemented that is commonly used on remote control boats and planes with similar dimensions
and power outputs to ours, called a servo based steering system. This system consists of few parts
including the servo itself, a mounting bracket, a servo arm, and a steering link. We chose to use
such a system because of the minimal number of parts and work required to make the system run
flawlessly. When the servo is connected to the transom of the boat, it will directly control the
movement of the outdrive. It does this simply by turning the output gear based on the input given by
the receiver. This output gear, of which the angle it turns can be very carefully altered with the
remote, is attached to the servo arm which translates the small rotational motion into an arc at the
end of the arm. The steering link is then connected to both the end of the servo arm and the linkage
on the outdrive. This push/pull on the outdrive by the servo causes it to turn at adequate speeds
with pinpoint precision.

pages.text:
UCONN
best interests, time and money wise, to use one of these propellers. The 3-blade propeller was
evaluated at an operating condition of 6000 RPM under identical simulation parameters as the 2blade configuration to enable a consistent comparison. The results indicate a total thrust
generation of approximately 6031 N and a corresponding torque requirement of 297 N·m. The
velocity streamline visualization, seen in Figure 1, demonstrates the formation of a strong and
continuous slipstream downstream of the propeller, indicating effective momentum transfer to the
fluid and a well-developed wake structure. The relatively uniform distribution of velocity within the
wake suggests consistent thrust production throughout the rotation cycle, which is desirable for
stable propulsion performance.
The pressure contour seen in Figure 2 further supports this behavior by showing a clear
pressure differential across the blade surfaces, with higher pressure on the pressure side and
lower pressure on the suction side. Due to the presence of three blades, the aerodynamic loading
is distributed more evenly across the propeller disk, reducing the load carried by each individual
blade. This more uniform load distribution contributes to smoother flow behavior and reduced
fluctuations in thrust. Additionally, the more continuous wake structure suggests reduced spatial
variation in the flow field, which can improve overall propulsion stability. However, the increased
blade area interacting with the fluid results in a higher torque requirement, indicating greater power
demand to achieve the same rotational speed.

The 2-blade propeller was analyzed under the same operating condition of 6000 RPM and
identical simulation setup to provide a direct basis for comparison. The simulation results show a
total thrust of approximately 4561 N and a torque requirement of 220 N·m. Compared to the 3blade configuration, the velocity streamline plot indicates a less uniform wake structure, with
greater variation in velocity distribution, shown in Figure 3, downstream of the propeller. This
suggests that the flow is influenced more strongly by individual blade passages, leading to a less
continuous slipstream and increased variation in the wake.
The pressure distribution in Figure 4 reveals more concentrated aerodynamic loading on
each blade, as the total force is carried by only two blades rather than being distributed across
three. This results in stronger localized pressure differences, particularly in regions near the blade
tips, where flow separation and vortex formation are more pronounced. While this configuration
reduces the overall torque required to rotate the propeller due to the decreased wet surface area, it
also leads to reduced thrust generation and less uniform flow characteristics. The more
intermittent wake structure may contribute to increased unsteadiness in the flow field, which can
negatively affect propulsion smoothness. Overall, the 2-blade propeller demonstrates lower power
demand but reduced performance in terms of thrust output and wake uniformity.

The next objective was to find the center of gravity and buoyancy of our boat. This was done by
finding the center of gravity in one direction. This was the x-direction. The x direction was chosen
because the model of the boat (figure 5) was symmetrical along the x-axis except for the indent of
into one of the walls. The value that was found by hand was -0.0321inches from the center of the
boat. This was compared to the value that was found using the SolidWorks center of gravity
solution tool. If the values matched, which they did, the SolidWorks center of gravity tool was able
to be used. The y and z directions were found using said tool. The local coordinates of the center of
gravity, in reference to the center of the SolidWorks model, were (-0.0321, 29.8009, 45.3292)
inches.

the middle, allow the boat to sit at the correct height and angle in the water while at rest and while
underway. We also sanded the entire hull down to wood and epoxied all bare surfaces to ensure
proper waterproofing on all surfaces.
Using a dual motor design with only one propellor means we needed to design a gearbox to
direct the power into a central driveshaft. We are completing this using ¼" steel plates to form a
rectangle that will house both motors, the drive shaft, and their corresponding gears. This
gear/motor box will be screwed to the top of the outdrive, connecting the motors' power to the
propellors. We are using a 2:1 gear ratio in the gearbox and a 1.5:1 gear ratio in the lower unit of the
outdrive. This brings the total rpms of the motors down from the rated 20,000 to above 6,000 at the
propellor, while increasing propellor torque in the process.

Customized Battery Creation
To address issues identified in previous year’s electrical design, the electrical engineering
team developed a custom battery pack intended to power two motors. The battery is configured as
a 13-series, 59 parallel (13S59P) system providing a nominal voltage of approximately 48 V and a
capacity of 94.4 Ah. The battery pack is spot welded together using nickel strips and separated into
modules where each module is connected to each other via copper plates and bars. The battery
pack will be connected to an Orion Jr 2 BMS to provide monitoring and safety protection.

Risk Assessment and Risk Cube
There are many risks associated with the execution of the boat. To summarize the most
important risks, the team has concluded that equipment malfunction, weather conditions, order
delays, and issues that may come up when traveling to the competition are the most likely to occur
and have impacts on the boat’s performance. Last year, the speed controller was compromised
and had to be replaced by a weaker part. To have the best performing boat, testing is critical to the
iterative process. With constantly varying weather conditions in Connecticut, testing parameters
will be impacted and may change results. A major issue that is currently being ironed out is order
delays and processing issues. A few parts have come up missing which delays the final execution
of the customized battery. Also, the second ESC has been delayed for administrative reasons. The
team hopes to continue preparation for the competition without the ESC and will have to determine
a course of action if the part does not arrive in time. One of the last-minute risks is any issues that

Design Approach
The design incorporates a fully waterproof battery enclosure to prevent electrical hazards and a
water-cooling system to manage heat buildup. A J-class hydroplane hull is used to improve stability
and reduce the likelihood of rolling or capsizing during operation.

Global Factors
Constraints Considered for this Factor
Growing worldwide interest in sustainable marine propulsion encourages the use of systems that
reduce fuel consumption and emissions. Component availability and cost can also be influenced
by global supply chains.

Design Approach
The project uses an electric propulsion system with an energy-efficient battery to eliminate fuel use
and greenhouse gas emissions. Simulation analysis is applied to reduce energy losses and improve
the system’s global sustainability alignment.

Cultural Factors
Constraints Considered for this Factor
Electric boat competitions emphasize fairness, innovation, and adherence to rules that ensure
equal opportunity among teams. Designs must reflect these expectations.

Design Approach
The mechanical steering and payload system is designed to mimic the function of a human driver
while meeting competition guidelines. This approach supports competitive integrity and aligns with
the culture of engineering innovation in student racing events.

Social Factors
Constraints Considered for this Factor
The project functions as an educational platform but comes with the challenge that many
stakeholders may not understand the risks or proper handling of electric propulsion systems. Clear
communication and safe operation are necessary.

Design Approach
Demonstration plans include straightforward explanations of system behavior, safety practices,
and educational materials that can be shared with students and the community to promote safe
and informed interaction with the vessel.

Environmental Factors
Constraints Considered for this Factor
Although electric propulsion reduces water pollution and fuel use, components such as batteries
and composite materials have their own environmental impacts. Waste generated during
fabrication must also be controlled.

Design Approach
Material waste is minimized during the build process, and all components, especially batteries, are
managed with proper disposal procedures. Efficiency improvements are targeted to reduce energy
draw and environmental impact over the vessel’s operating life.

Economic Factors
Constraints Considered for this Factor
The project operates under a limited budget, requiring cost-effective material and component
choices. Excessive prototyping or unnecessary tooling increases expenses.

Design Approach
Cost analysis influences all material and component decisions, favoring options that are durable
yet affordable. CFD and simulation reduce the need for physical prototypes, and the system is
designed for long-term maintainability so future teams can reuse or build upon the design.
